openings_only.what_it_means: the headline. Door pairs the control did not already produce, so every pair counted needed a doorway in the floor to be reported. Read `recall` through `recall_is_label_contact_not_detection` before quoting it.

openings_only_all_pairs.what_it_means: the same scoring without the control subtracted. Published for comparison only: both its numerator and its denominator contain pairs the rasterisation hands over for free. This is also the configuration the no-skill baseline is scored against, since the baseline has no control to subtract.

recall_is_label_contact_not_detection.what_it_means: recall 0.9858 is NOT a detection rate. fill_nearest grows each room's label through free space, so wherever the annotated floor joins two rooms their labels MUST come into contact, and openings() reports a pair on contact. Of the 141 live truth pairs, 138 have their two rooms joined by walkable floor and 138 of those 138 were predicted -- all of them. The 2 misses are pairs the rasterisation left in different free-space components, 0 of them joined by walkable floor. The only part of openings() that can refuse a pair it has contact for is the width filter (> 2.5 x DOOR_MAX_M is discarded as a whole open side); it discarded 6 pairs here, 0 of them real door pairs. So recall measures the annotation's own floor connectivity, not discrimination by openings(). The discriminating number is precision 0.6915 on 62 false positives. A further 1 truth pair(s) were predicted with no walkable floor between the two rooms at all, which is the same wall-bridging the negative control measures rather than a door being found.

annotated_door_widths.note: every door the truth derivation placed on a scored storey, as annotated. Published because DOOR_MAX_M is the constant the with_splitter block fails on, so the distribution it is being compared against must be visible rather than summarised as a modal band.

no_skill_baseline.note: a predictor that never runs openings(): call two annotated rooms adjacent when their drawn floor polygons come within d metres of each other. It reads only truth-side geometry. Scored against the same unsubtracted truth as openings_only_all_pairs, because it has no control to subtract.
no_skill_baseline.what_it_means: the best no-skill radius scores f1 0.547 against openings()' 0.7338 on the same truth, so the headline is not a restatement of the annotation's geometry. It is the margin that makes the result non-tautological, and it is published here rather than claimed.

control.note: openings() run on the same storeys with every doorway reveal deleted from the floor. These pairs are reported with no doorway present to report, so they measure the rasterisation and the 5x5 contact dilation, not the code's ability to find a door. They are removed from both sides of the headline score.

effect_of_subtracting_it.note: which direction the control moved the published numbers. Stated explicitly because subtracting a negative control is usually a penalty and here it is not: it removes far more false positives than true positives.
effect_of_subtracting_it.what_it_means: subtracting the control RAISED precision 0.5833 -> 0.6915, RAISED f1 0.7338 -> 0.8129 and RAISED exact-graph storeys 3 -> 6 of 28. Only recall fell, 0.9887 -> 0.9858. The control is not a handicap the result survived; it is a correction that improved every reading but one, because the 101 pairs it removes are mostly pairs openings() should not have reported (36 of them were real door pairs).

how_separable_the_annotated_rooms_are.note: the annotated rooms, against the number of separate floor regions left when every doorway reveal is deleted. This bounds any room splitter that works from floor coverage: rooms that share a floor region with no boundary between them cannot be told apart from the floor alone. It is a measurement of the DATA, so it is also the figure that says whether a poor room count is the data's fault or ours.
how_separable_the_annotated_rooms_are.what_it_means: 255 of 292 annotated rooms (87.3%) ARE separated by drawn geometry once the doorway reveals are removed, so the data imposes almost no ceiling here. split_rooms() recovers 47 of them, rising to 170 when the erosion is widened from DOOR_MAX_M = 0.70 m to 0.90 m. A splitter that merges rooms the geometry separates is failing for its own reasons, not against a limit in the annotation.

false_positives.note: pairs reported only when the doorways are present, that no annotated door joins. Read with care: the truth here is DOORS, and openings() reports open connections too by design, so a pair that two rooms genuinely share through an archway counts against it. wall_gap_m is the thinnest non-floor between the two room polygons, which does NOT separate the two cases -- a pair joined by a door is also walled everywhere else -- so no mechanical split of these is offered. They are listed per storey instead.

what_this_validates: openings() given PERFECT room geometry and perfect room identity: the floor polygons are drawn by a human, so nothing here is sensed, fused or segmented.

That the opening list keys the right pairs of rooms: 139 of 141 door pairs across 28 storeys of 16 real buildings, with the raster's own free pairs subtracted first. The 2 it misses are named per storey under `missed`. This is a KEYING result, not a detection result -- see the next entry.

That the opening decision beats a no-skill reading of the same geometry. Thresholding the distance between the drawn room polygons scores f1 at best 0.547 (at d = 0.20 m) against openings()' 0.7338 on the same unsubtracted truth, so the headline is not the annotation restated.
That the width filter -- width > 2.5 x DOOR_MAX_M is discarded as a whole open side -- throws away no real doorway in this set: it discarded 6 pairs, of which 0 were real door pairs.
A-ADJ, which compliance_matrix.md row 2.2 reports as having no ground truth of any kind. It now has one, at the unit level only.
what_this_does_not_validate: The pipeline end to end. There is no capture in this dataset. Depth, poses, fusion, floor finding, wall finding and room splitting are all bypassed. Nothing here says a plan built from a real walk has the right adjacency.

RECALL AS A DETECTION RATE. recall 0.9858 must not be read as "openings() found 139 of 141 doors". fill_nearest grows each room's label through free space, so label contact is GUARANTEED wherever the annotated floor joins two rooms. Of the 141 live truth pairs, 138 are so joined and 138 of those were predicted; the 2 misses are pairs the rasterisation left in different free-space components. The width filter, the only part of openings() that can refuse a pair it has contact for, fired on 0 truth pairs. Recall therefore measures the annotation's floor connectivity. The number that measures openings() is precision 0.6915, on 62 false positives.

Room splitting. In the headline configuration the room labels ARE the annotation, so split_rooms() does not run. This benchmark does not excuse it. The with_splitter block runs it on the same perfect floor and it recovers almost nothing -- recall 0.0284, 4 of 141 pairs -- because DOOR_MAX_M is 0.70 m while the 273 doors annotated here run 0.53 to 1.88 m with a median of 0.80 m and 90.5% of them wider than 0.70 m (26 are at or below it). An erosion sized for 0.70 m never pinches most of those off and most storeys come back as a single room. room_count_if_door_max_were_0.90_m is published per storey as evidence for that reading. It is NOT a proposal to change the constant: 0.70 was set on our own captures and would need its own measurement to move.

Opening WIDTH. What openings() measures is the clear width of the floor neck, which is not the door leaf the dataset annotates. The two are not compared. door_width_m is published per storey for the reader only.

Anything about our own captures. These are large American houses as a drawn annotation; the UK flats the pipeline is built for are not represented, and their doors are narrower, which is exactly the constant that fails above.

Precision in the ordinary sense. The truth here is DOORS, and openings() is documented to report open connections too. 60 of the 62 false positives are pairs whose labels meet ONLY inside a floor patch the annotation drew inside a wall and named no door on -- an opening the dataset shows but does not label. The same flag fires on 0 of the 139 true positives, so it is not a blanket excuse; but it does mean the reported precision is a lower bound and the true figure against real adjacency is unmeasured.
controls_run: Negative control: every storey is also scored with the doorway reveals deleted from the floor, so no doorway exists to find. openings() still reports 101 pairs, 36 of them real door pairs. Their room polygons sit 0-7 cm apart (35 of them touch outright, so the annotation drew no partition there at all; the other 66 are across a thin wall) and the 5x5 contact dilation in openings() reaches 4 cm from each label, so it bridges them. All 101 are subtracted from both sides of the headline.

Which direction that subtraction moved the result, because a reader may assume a control is a handicap. It is not one here: precision 0.5833 -> 0.6915, f1 0.7338 -> 0.8129 and exact-graph storeys 3 -> 6 all ROSE; only recall fell, 0.9887 -> 0.9858. The full statement is in summary.control.effect_of_subtracting_it.

That bridging is a real property of the code, not of this dataset: openings() has no minimum width, so a pair bridged across a wall is published into plan.adjacency with a width near zero. On our own 2 cm grid any partition thinner than about 8 cm of unobserved floor is at risk.
The doorless-reveal flag is reported for the true positives as well as the false ones, so a flag that fired on everything would be visible.
A no-skill baseline on the truth side's own geometry, at 4 radii, so the headline can be compared against doing nothing. Best f1 0.547 against 0.7338.
truth_derivation: The dataset has no room entities and no door-to-room association; both are derived in bench/houselayout3d.py from the annotation alone.
A room is a floor-facing horizontal entity of at least ROOM_MIN_AREA_M2, which is our own constant. A different threshold would give a different room set.

A door's two rooms are found by stepping off the rectangle along its annotated normal. Doors that find a room on one side are counted as exterior and dropped; doors that find the same room on both sides mean the annotation did not split that space, and are dropped too. Both counts are published per storey.
